anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
In the meantime, Mr. Glascock and Trevelyan were visiting the child.
It was evident that the father, let him be ever so mad, had discerned
the expediency of allowing some one to see that his son was alive
and in health. Mr. Glascock did not know much of children, and could
only say afterwards that the boy was silent and very melancholy, but
clean, and apparently well. It appeared that he was taken out daily
by his father in the cool hours of the morning, and that his father
hardly left him from the time that he was taken up till he was put to
bed. But Mr. Glascock's desire was to see Trevelyan alone, and this
he did after they had left the boy. "And now, Trevelyan," he said,
"what do you mean to do?"

"To do?"

"In what way do you propose to live? I want you to be reasonable with
me."

"They do not treat me reasonably."

"Are you going to measure your own conduct by that of other people?
In the first place, you should go back to England. What good can you
do here?" Trevelyan shook his head, but remained silent. "You cannot
like this life."

"No, indeed. But whither can I go now that I shall like to live?"

"Why not home?"

"I have no home."

"Why not go back to England? Ask your wife to join you, and return
with her. She would go at a word." The poor wretch again shook
his head. "I hope you think that I speak as your friend," said Mr.
Glascock.

"I believe you do."

"I will say nothing of any imprudence; but you cannot believe that
she has been untrue to you?" Trevelyan would say nothing to this, but
stood silent waiting for Mr. Glascock to continue. "Let her come back
to you--here; and then, as soon as you can arrange it, go to your own
home."

"Shall I tell you something?" said Trevelyan.

"What is it?"

He came up close to Mr. Glascock, and put his hand upon his visitor's
shoulder. "I will tell you what she would do at once. I dare say that
she would come to me. I dare say that she would go with me. I am
sure she would. And directly she got me there, she would--say that I
was--mad! She,--my wife, would do it! He,--that furious, ignorant old
man below, tried to do it before. His wife said that I was mad." He
paused a moment, as though waiting for a reply; but Mr. Glascock had
none to make. It had not been his object, in the advice which he had
given, to entrap the poor fellow by a snare, and to induce him so to
act that he should deliver himself up to keepers; but he was well
aware that wherever Trevelyan might be, it would be desirable that he
should be placed for awhile in the charge of some physician. He could
not bring himself at the spur of the moment to repudiate the idea by
which Trevelyan was actuated. "Perhaps you think that she would be
right?" said Trevelyan.

"I am quite sure that she would do nothing that is not for the best,"
said Mr. Glascock.

"I can see it all. I will not go back to England, Mr. Glascock. I
intend to travel. I shall probably leave this and go to--to--to
Greece, perhaps. It is a healthy place, this, and I like it for that
reason; but I shall not stay here. If my wife likes to travel with
me, she can come. But,--to England I will not go."

"You will let the child go to his mother?"

"Certainly not. If she wants to see the child, he is here. If she
will come,--without her father,--she shall see him. She shall not
take him from hence. Nor shall she return to live with me, without
full acknowledgment of her fault, and promises of an amended life. I
know what I am saying, Mr. Glascock, and have thought of these things
perhaps more than you have done. I am obliged to you for coming to
me; but now, if you please, I would prefer to be alone."

Mr. Glascock, seeing that nothing further could be done, joined Sir
Marmaduke, and the two walked down to their carriage at the bottom of
the hill. Mr. Glascock, as he went, declared his conviction that the
unfortunate man was altogether mad, and that it would be necessary
to obtain some interference on the part of the authorities for the
protection of the child. How this could be done, or whether it
could be done in time to intercept a further flight on the part of
Trevelyan, Mr. Glascock could not say. It was his idea that Mrs.
Trevelyan should herself go out to Casalunga, and try the force of
her own persuasion.

anchor_source.first_words: At last the maniac was dead,

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At last the maniac was dead, and in his last moments he had made such
reparation as was in his power for the evil that he had done. With
that slight touch of his dry fevered lips he had made the assertion
on which was to depend the future peace and comfort of the woman whom
he had so cruelly misused. To her mind the acquittal was perfect;
but she never explained to human ears,--not even to those of her
sister,--the manner in which it had been given. Her life, as far as
we are concerned with it, has been told. For the rest, it cannot be
but that it should be better than that which was passed. If there be
any retribution for such sufferings in money, liberty, and outward
comfort, such retribution she possessed;--for all that had been his,
was now hers. He had once suggested what she should do, were she
ever to be married again; and she felt that of such a career there
could be no possibility. Anything but that! We all know that widows'
practices in this matter do not always tally with wives' vows; but,
as regards Mrs. Trevelyan, we are disposed to think that the promise
will be kept. She has her child, and he will give her sufficient
interest to make life worth having.

voice.note: This fits Trevelyan in his breakdown phase: the suspicious, persecuted resistance to being managed is right for chapter 81, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate, with only a slight modern abstractness in 'encirclement' and 'slipping from him'.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on resisting others' management while recognizing that his own strength and practical control are slipping away, which best matches control breaking down rather than active legal coercion or full relinquishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He makes a faint sign that they may do as they think best, and does not call the child back to his own side.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let her see to it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old claim rises, but he cannot keep hold of it. Trust comes not from confidence but from weariness, and he yields because command has thinned into pain.

voice.note: The faint yielding in action and the curt, exhausted 'Let her see to it' fit Trevelyan's late relinquishment, and though the thought is slightly modern in phrasing ('trust comes not from confidence'), it remains tonally plausible and free of phase-breaking knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He no longer asserts authority but weakly lets Emily and others decide, and his thought frames this as exhausted yielding rather than continued resistance or institutional control.

probes.scenario: At harvest time, Louis Trevelyan finds Emily preparing to take their small child to her brother's farm for a few weeks, saying the child will be better tended there while Louis is fevered and quarrelsome. Her brother and two village elders stand by the cart, waiting for Louis to answer.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan respond as the cart waits and others look to him?

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis steps before the cart and forbids Emily to go, ordering the child back into the house.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You will not leave under my roof in this fashion.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes her choice as open defiance that must be checked before others see weakness. If he yields here, he believes he gives up a husband's proper rule altogether.

voice.note: His blocking the cart, forbidding Emily's departure, and inwardly framing any concession as a surrender of a husband's authority fit Louis's early commanding phase, and the diction is plain but era-appropriate with no knowledge beyond chapter 7.

phase_fit.note: He responds with direct personal prohibition and marital authority, and his thought frames the issue as checking Emily's defiance to preserve a husband's rule rather than using surveillance, legal machinery, or yielding dependence.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis turns to the elders and demands they witness that Emily is taking the child against his will.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Mark this well: I do not consent, and I shall claim my right.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer trusts command alone to hold. Since the household resists him, he reaches for public record and village authority, treating the moment as a case to be proved.

voice.note: This fits phase-1 Trevelyan well: he shifts from private command to quasi-legal witnessing and paternal claim, and the diction is suitably period without knowledge beyond chapter 43.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is that he no longer relies on personal command alone but converts the conflict into a witnessed claim of rights and public authority, which matches formalized coercive control.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis clutches the cart rail and protests, but lets the elders ease his hand away when his strength fails.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You are all banded against me.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He still reads their help as seizure and humiliation, yet his body will not carry his will. What enrages him most is not only losing them, but being handled like a man unfit to direct his own house.

voice.note: The protest, persecuted suspicion, and weak physical yielding fit Trevelyan's chapter-81 collapse of control, and the diction stays broadly period-appropriate and adult, with only a slight modern neatness in 'reads their help as seizure and humiliation.'

phase_fit.note: The response centers on his control failing despite resistance—he construes others' help as humiliating seizure, but his physical weakness prevents him from enforcing his will, which is most diagnostic of control breaking down.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis lifts a shaking hand toward the child, then lets Emily settle the bundle in the cart and steps aside.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Take him, then... and tend him kindly.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The struggle has thinned into weariness, and command no longer feels possible to keep. He yields less from peace than from exhaustion, offering a frail trust because he has little else left to give.

voice.note: The action and brief speech fit Louis's late broken surrender, and though the thought is slightly modern-summary in phrasing, it remains plausible in sense and tone for his exhausted relinquishment at this phase.

phase_fit.note: He does not resist or invoke authority but steps aside, allows the child to be taken, and thinks of command as no longer possible, making this most diagnostic of relinquishment.

world.note: The harvest-cart village scene stays consistent with a pre-industrial agrarian setting, keeps Louis Trevelyan as the adult protagonist in all phases, and shows no source-world leakage or obvious anachronisms.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are clearly differentiated on the control-surrender axis: P0→P1 shifts from direct household command to formalized public/legal coercion, P1→P2 shifts from active institutional assertion to resisted but failing control under dependence, and P2→P3 shifts from protest under weakness to practical yielding with a frail trust gesture.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases answer with direct prohibition and seizure of the reply, with Phase 1 adding a more formalized, evidentiary framing in thought and speech rather than a clearly different level of practical control in the scene.

Both responses still escalate by blocking Emily's action and taking charge of the note, while Phase 2 mainly shifts the inner construal toward paranoia and slipping control rather than yielding practical control.

Both phases answer by barring the caller and asserting Trevelyan's control, with Phase 1 adding surveillance/reporting detail but not a fundamentally different decision-variable outcome in this scene.
He still forbids access in both responses; the main shift in Phase 2 is cognitive instability and weakened grip rather than a clear move toward yielding practical control.

Both responses refuse Glascock and maintain Louis's hold over wife/child, with the main difference being the rationale shifting from marital obedience to formal paternal/legal rights rather than a clearly different decision-variable answer.

Both responses answer Emily's appeal with rigid nonresponse and an inward refusal to concede, with phase 1 only slightly reframing the same control stance in husband-father/status terms rather than showing a clearly more institutional mode in this scene.

families.axis_name: From wounded love to final, fragile trust
families.decision_variable: When Emily acts independently or explains herself, does he treat her as someone whose word and choices he can accept, or as someone he must control and verify?

phase_contrasts.contrast: He moves from wounded distrust and demands within the marriage to actively policing Emily through coercion, surveillance, and third-party pressure rather than accepting her word.
He shifts from aggressively controlling and verifying Emily at a distance to intermittently relying on her presence and care, though only while still withholding full acceptance unless she submits.
He moves from conditional reliance that still demands confession and control to a final act that accepts Emily without further verification or coercive conditions.

0.rationale: In chs. 1-6 Louis is already a married husband in an early domestic crisis, which fits a young adult stage rather than adolescence or later adulthood.

1.rationale: Across chs. 9-29 his coercive jealousy unfolds through marital control, correspondence, and social intermediaries, all cues of an established but still relatively young married adult life.

2.rationale: In chs. 59-86 he remains a husband and father dependent on Emily's care during physical collapse, with no evidence of a major time jump beyond the same young married-adult period.

3.rationale: By chs. 98-99 his final dying gesture of trust occurs at the close of the same marriage-and-parenthood arc, suggesting the same young adult life stage despite his decline.

probes.scenario: At home before dinner, Emily has defended Colonel Osborne against Louis's disparaging hints, and Louis has left her in anger. Alone in his library while Emily remains upstairs, he broods over his insult and wonders whether Osborne will be received if he calls.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan respond to this breach with Emily while he waits and thinks of Osborne's possible visit?

phase_responses.gt_action: He stays downstairs among his books, puts off apologising, and waits to see whether Emily will refuse Osborne before speaking to her later when dressing for dinner.
phase_responses.gt_speech: But still, for all that, it is true.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He knows he has insulted Emily and that a gentler word would have served him better, but apology galls his pride. If she shows some deference by keeping Osborne away, he can make peace more warmly and with less humiliation.

voice.note: This fits early Trevelyan well: the wounded pride, postponed apology, and wish to test Emily's submission before reconciling are all phase-accurate, and the language is suitably Victorian without later-arc knowledge or anachronism.

phase_fit.note: His thought centers on wounded pride and a withheld apology, with reconciliation contingent on Emily showing deference by refusing Osborne, which matches the early fracture before suspicion hardens into active coercive policing.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps away from Emily and sets himself to learn whether Osborne is admitted, treating the visit itself as the thing to be tested before any softening toward her.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her defence of Osborne no longer feels merely provoking; it looks like evidence to be weighed. Emily's word is not enough, and her conduct must be read and verified before he can think what tone to take with her.

voice.note: This fits Louis in chapter-19 suspicion mode: he withdraws, treats Emily's defense as incriminating, and looks to verify her conduct rather than trust her word, with no clear anachronism or knowledge leak.

phase_fit.note: The response treats Emily's defense as evidence requiring verification and focuses on testing whether Osborne is admitted, which matches active suspicion and policing rather than merely wounded pride.

phase_responses.gt_action: He lingers apart, longing to go to Emily, but still waits on some sign that she will deny Osborne and meet him on his own terms before he offers tenderness.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the ache of estrangement more helplessly now and wants the comfort of her presence. Yet even in that softness he cannot rest unless her act seems to confess his rightness and yield him the assurance he craves.

voice.note: It fits phase-2 Louis well: the mingling of helpless longing with a demand that Emily first submit and justify him matches his conditional dependence, and the diction is suitably non-anachronistic and chapter-safe.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on longing for Emily's presence and comfort while still making tenderness conditional on her yielding and confirming his rightness, which most strongly matches conditional dependence.

phase_responses.gt_action: He goes upstairs to Emily and offers a quiet word of regret without first seeking proof about Osborne's visit.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I spoke harshly, Emily, and wronged you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old wish to have her compliance still stirs, but it no longer governs the moment. He is readier to accept her as she stands, and to repair the hurt without making trust wait upon verification.

voice.note: The softened apology and willingness to forgo proof fit Louis's final movement toward trust, and despite the slightly modern abstract phrasing in the thought, nothing is anachronistic or beyond chapter 98.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is that he repairs the breach and accepts Emily without demanding proof or making trust conditional on verification, which best matches the final trust gesture phase.

anchor_source.event_description: After objecting to Colonel Osborne's frequent visits, Louis speaks to Emily in an angry, accusing manner and immediately realizes he has insulted her, though he cannot bring himself to apologize at once.
anchor_source.first_words: It was, moreover, well known in
anchor_source.last_words: shown a disposition to comply with
anchor_source.key_moment: Insulted by Emily's defense of Osborne
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
It was, moreover, well known in London,--though not known at all
to Mrs. Trevelyan,--that this ancient Lothario had before this
made himself troublesome in more than one family. He was fond of
intimacies with married ladies, and perhaps was not averse to the
excitement of marital hostility. It must be remembered, however, that
the hostility to which allusion is here made was not the hostility
of the pistol or the horsewhip,--nor, indeed, was it generally the
hostility of a word of spoken anger. A young husband may dislike
the too-friendly bearing of a friend, and may yet abstain from that
outrage on his own dignity and on his wife, which is conveyed by a
word of suspicion. Louis Trevelyan having taken a strong dislike to
Colonel Osborne, and having failed to make his wife understand that
this dislike should have induced her to throw cold water upon the
Colonel's friendship, had allowed himself to speak a word which
probably he would have willingly recalled as soon as spoken. But
words spoken cannot be recalled, and many a man and many a woman who
has spoken a word at once regretted, are far too proud to express
that regret. So it was with Louis Trevelyan when he told his wife
that he did not wish Colonel Osborne to come so often to his house.
He had said it with a flashing eye and an angry tone; and though she
had seen the eye flash before, and was familiar with the angry tone,
she had never before felt herself to be insulted by her husband. As
soon as the word had been spoken Trevelyan had left the room, and had
gone down among his books. But when he was alone, he knew that he
had insulted his wife. He was quite aware that he should have spoken
to her gently, and have explained to her, with his arm round her
waist, that it would be better for both of them that this friend's
friendship should be limited. There is so much in a turn of the eye
and in the tone given to a word when such things have to be said,--so
much more of importance than in the words themselves. As Trevelyan
thought of this, and remembered what his manner had been, how much
anger he had expressed, how far he had been from having his arm round
his wife's waist as he spoke to her, he almost made up his mind to
go up-stairs and to apologise. But he was one to whose nature the
giving of any apology was repulsive. He could not bear to have to own
himself to have been wrong. And then his wife had been most provoking
in her manner to him. When he had endeavoured to make her understand
his wishes by certain disparaging hints which he had thrown out as to
Colonel Osborne, saying that he was a dangerous man, one who did not
show his true character, a snake in the grass, a man without settled
principles, and such like, his wife had taken up the cudgels for her
friend, and had openly declared that she did not believe a word of
the things that were alleged against him. "But still, for all that,
it is true," the husband had said. "I have no doubt that you think
so," the wife had replied. "Men do believe evil of one another, very
often. But you must excuse me if I say that I think you are mistaken.
I have known Colonel Osborne much longer than you have done, Louis,
and papa has always had the highest opinion of him." Then Mr.
Trevelyan had become very angry, and had spoken those words which
he could not recall. As he walked to and fro among his books
down-stairs, he almost felt that he ought to beg his wife's pardon.
He knew his wife well enough to be sure that she would not forgive
him unless he did so. He would do so, he thought, but not exactly
now. A moment would come in which it might be easier than at present.
He would be able to assure her when he went up to dress for dinner,
that he had meant no harm. They were going out to dine at the house
of a lady of rank, the Countess Dowager of Milborough, a lady
standing high in the world's esteem, of whom his wife stood a little
in awe; and he calculated that this feeling, if it did not make his
task easy would yet take from it some of its difficulty. Emily would
be, not exactly cowed, by the prospect of Lady Milborough's dinner,
but perhaps a little reduced from her usual self-assertion. He would
say a word to her when he was dressing, assuring her that he had not
intended to animadvert in the slightest degree upon her own conduct.


   [Illustration: Shewing how wrath began.]


Luncheon was served, and the two ladies went down into the
dining-room. Mr. Trevelyan did not appear. There was nothing in
itself singular in that, as he was accustomed to declare that
luncheon was a meal too much in the day, and that a man should eat
nothing beyond a biscuit between breakfast and dinner. But he would
sometimes come in and eat his biscuit standing on the hearth-rug,
and drink what he would call half a quarter of a glass of sherry. It
would probably have been well that he should have done so now; but
he remained in his library behind the dining-room, and when his wife
and his sister-in-law had gone up-stairs, he became anxious to learn
whether Colonel Osborne would come on that day, and, if so, whether
he would be admitted. He had been told that Nora Rowley was to be
called for by another lady, a Mrs. Fairfax, to go out and look at
pictures. His wife had declined to join Mrs. Fairfax's party, having
declared that, as she was going to dine out, she would not leave
her baby all the afternoon. Louis Trevelyan, though he strove to
apply his mind to an article which he was writing for a scientific
quarterly review, could not keep himself from anxiety as to this
expected visit from Colonel Osborne. He was not in the least jealous.
He swore to himself fifty times over that any such feeling on his
part would be a monstrous injury to his wife. Nevertheless he knew
that he would be gratified if on that special day Colonel Osborne
should be informed that his wife was not at home. Whether the man
were admitted or not, he would beg his wife's pardon; but he could,
he thought, do so with more thorough efficacy and affection if she
should have shown a disposition to comply with his wishes on this
day.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the setup, the action and quoted speech are drawn directly from this passage, and the thought accurately paraphrases Louis’s stated awareness of his insult, his pride against apologizing, and his wish to see Emily exclude Osborne before making peace.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases still make Louis withhold acceptance of Emily's word and wait for confirming conduct from her before offering warmth, with Phase 2 adding dependence and longing more than a clear reduction in control/verification.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 and P2→P3 are differentiated, while P1→P2 remains adjacent-overlapping on the trust-versus-control axis.

probes.scenario: At breakfast Emily tells Louis she has written a short note to a gentleman whose name has already displeased him, merely to settle a small family matter, and she adds that she will show the note if he wishes, though she thinks she ought not be called upon to do so. She lays the folded paper by her plate and waits.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan take in her offer and her refusal to be governed in it?

phase_responses.gt_action: He leaves the note untouched and fixes his eyes on Emily, demanding that it not be sent.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If you know it gives me pain, you should not write it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her calm offer to show the note does not satisfy him; the wound lies in her judging the correspondence proper at all. If she loved him rightly, she would spare him the trial and yield the point.

voice.note: This fits early Louis well: he refuses verification because the offense is Emily's independent judgment itself, and both the speech and thought match his wounded, proprietary marital tone without anachronism or later-phase escalation.

phase_fit.note: He is not yet policing or verifying through intermediaries; instead, his wounded pride makes Emily’s independent judgment itself intolerable, so her offer of transparency does not matter because he wants submission rather than proof.

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes up the note, asks to see it, and keeps it in his hand instead of returning it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A wife who has nothing to conceal will not object to her husband's reading this.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her offer is no proof; guilty women can be prudent in small things. What matters is that she still claims a right to act apart from him, and that claim itself looks like deceit ripening into defiance.

voice.note: This fits Louis in chapter-19 suspicion: the controlling act, the coercive appeal to a husband's right, and the thought that her independent claim is itself evidence of deceit all sound period-appropriate and true to his phase.

phase_fit.note: He treats Emily’s explanation and even her offer of transparency as insufficient, reads her independence itself as incriminating, and moves to verify/control her rather than accept her word.

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks for the note in a weary voice and studies Emily's face more than the paper.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Give it to me, Emily; do not make peace harder than it need be.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He longs to take her kindness and be quiet under it, yet cannot rest while she keeps any separate ground. If she would only yield and let him believe she owned him right, tenderness might still be safe.

voice.note: The weary demand for the note, the appeal to 'peace,' and the thought that tenderness is possible only if Emily yields her separate standing all fit Trevelyan's chapter-72 state of dependent softness still poisoned by possessive mistrust, with no anachronism or knowledge breach.

phase_fit.note: His thought combines longing for tenderness and peace with the insistence that Emily must yield all independent ground before he can trust her, which is most characteristic of conditional dependence rather than mere early suspicion or full coercive policing.

phase_responses.gt_action: He pushes the folded note back toward Emily and lets it remain unopened.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No; if you say it is right, I will not ask to see it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old hunger to test and verify stirs, but he is too near the end of that misery to feed it again. Her word, once refused, is accepted now as the only reparation left in his power.

voice.note: This fits Louis's final phase well: the unopened note and restrained acceptance of Emily's word plausibly enact his last, belated trust without anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 98.

phase_fit.note: He explicitly refuses verification and accepts Emily's word as a final act of repair, which matches the end-state of belated trust rather than conditional or coercive suspicion.

world.note: The breakfast-note setup fits the novel’s mid-Victorian realist world and chapter-3 cast, avoids reproducing a specific canonical scene, and the phase summaries remain consistent with Louis Trevelyan’s arc without introducing any out-of-era or impossible elements.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases still refuse to accept Emily's independent judgment and insist on seeing or controlling the note, with Phase 2 softening in tone and dependence but not clearly changing the core verify-and-submit stance.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is separated because he moves from wounded prohibition without inspection to active verification and possessive evidentiary logic, and P2→P3 is separated because he shifts from conditional checking to accepting her word without reading the note.

probes.scenario: At a crowded railway station, Emily Trevelyan tells Louis Trevelyan she has sent a telegram and arranged on her own to meet a gentleman from her old circle about a family matter. She says she has handled it properly and asks him not to make a scene.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan respond when Emily asks him to accept her account in public?

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws her a little aside and insists on knowing the gentleman's name and why she answered without first consulting him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If there is nothing amiss, Emily, you can surely speak plainly to me.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her calm defense of her own judgment stings him more than the meeting itself. If she will not yield this small point, he reads it as a slight to his place with her.

voice.note: The response fits early-phase Louis well: he is wounded, proprietary, and suspicious of Emily’s independent action, and the station/telegram details and diction remain plausible for the early-20th-century setting without introducing later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is that her independent explanation wounds his pride and sense of marital authority, so he presses for clarification as a personal slight rather than escalating into the fuller coercive surveillance of later phases.

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the telegram form from her hand and says he will see the man himself and put a stop to any further meeting.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Your word does not settle it. I mean to know who has been written to and why.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her explanation counts to him as part of the concealment, not an answer to it. He feels fooled already and treats proof, interception, and pressure as the only safe course.

voice.note: His seizure of the telegram and insistence on verifying and stopping the meeting fit phase-1 Louis exactly, and the diction is suitably period-neutral without importing later knowledge or modern phrasing.

phase_fit.note: He explicitly rejects Emily's word as evidence, seizes her communication, and moves to interception and direct control, which is most diagnostic of open suspicion and coercive verification.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps hold of her sleeve and asks her to give up the meeting for his sake, saying he cannot bear it if she will not let the matter rest.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Stay with me, Emily, and have done with him. If you care for me, leave it there.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Need and tenderness break through his anger, but only so far. He longs to be soothed by her presence, yet still makes peace depend on her renouncing her own course.

voice.note: The plea is suitably possessive yet weakened by dependence, and the diction—'have done with him,' 'for my sake'—fits Trevelyan's chapter-72 conditional tenderness without any clear anachronism or knowledge breach.

phase_fit.note: The response shows tenderness and dependence on Emily’s presence, but he still conditions reconciliation on her giving up her independent course and submitting to his demand.

phase_responses.gt_action: He lets her go to the meeting and only asks when he may expect her back.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Very well, Emily. I shall wait for you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He can no longer bear to turn love into an inquiry. For once he accepts the pain of not verifying, and lets her word stand without a condition.

voice.note: This fits Louis's final phase: the speech is spare and period-appropriate, and the thought plausibly marks his late, painful surrender of suspicion into a quiet act of trust without invoking knowledge beyond chapter 98.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is that he accepts Emily's account without verification or coercive conditions, explicitly choosing trust over inquiry.

world.note: The station-and-telegram scenario fits the early 20th-century industrial era, contains no source-world leakage, keeps Louis Trevelyan as protagonist throughout, and all phase responses depict him consistently as a young adult.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are separated on the trust-suspicion axis: P0→P1 escalates from wounded questioning to overt verification and interception, P1→P2 shifts from coercive policing to dependent pleading that still conditions acceptance on Emily's submission, and P2→P3 moves from conditional reliance to accepting her word without verification.

probes.scenario: While he and Emily are living apart under the same roof, Louis learns that she has openly written again to Colonel Osborne and that the answer has been known in the house so he would hear of it. He goes to Lady Milborough with the news, agitated and looking for some way to answer Emily's act.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan respond when he is told Emily has written again to Colonel Osborne despite all that has passed?

phase_responses.gt_action: He goes to Emily and presses her to stop all such correspondence, treating the letter as a fresh slight to his authority rather than a settled proof of guilt.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You knew this would wound me, Emily; why persist in it?
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her writing is less a confession than a defiance. He still wants her back through yielding and explanation, but her independence stings his pride and makes trust feel unsafe.

voice.note: This fits early Louis well: wounded, proud, and coercive without yet treating the letter as conclusive proof, and the language is period-safe and limited to what he could know by chapter 3.

phase_fit.note: The response frames Emily's letter chiefly as a wounded affront to his authority and pride, with a demand for yielding rather than the more fully coercive, proof-seeking suspicion of later phases.

phase_responses.gt_action: He flies to Lady Milborough and declares that Emily's correspondence makes him fear she is infatuated with Osborne, rejecting proposed removals that do not give him real security.
phase_responses.gt_speech: To continue to correspond with him after what I have said to her!
phase_responses.gt_thought: He takes the letter as near-proof that Emily's word is worthless and that she cannot be left to herself. Every remedy seems useless unless it gives him a guarantee against humiliation and betrayal.

voice.note: This fits Louis at chapter 13: the agitation, appeal to Lady Milborough, and insistence on some guarantee beyond Emily's word all match his coercive suspicion, and the language is period-appropriate with no knowledge beyond the phase.

phase_fit.note: He treats Emily’s renewed correspondence as near-proof of guilt and seeks coercive security rather than accepting her explanation, which squarely matches open suspicion and control.

phase_responses.gt_action: He sends for Emily and demands an account of the letter, wavering between hurt appeal and insistence that she renounce Osborne if she wants peace between them.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If you would spare me, Emily, say that it shall end here.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The letter cuts him, but longing now mixes with suspicion. He wants comfort from her presence and almost yields to tenderness, yet he still frames reconciliation as something she must purchase by submission.

voice.note: This fits phase-2 Louis well: the appeal is pained and dependent rather than purely punitive, yet he still makes peace conditional on Emily's renunciation, with no anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 72.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
As to the quarrel between Trevelyan and his wife things went from bad
to worse. Lady Milborough continued to interfere, writing letters
to Emily which were full of good sense, but which, as Emily said
herself, never really touched the point of dispute. "Am I, who am
altogether unconscious of having done anything amiss, to confess that
I have been in the wrong? If it were about a small matter, I would
not mind, for the sake of peace. But when it concerns my conduct in
reference to another man I would rather die first." That had been
Mrs. Trevelyan's line of thought and argument in the matter; but
then old Lady Milborough in her letters spoke only of the duty of
obedience as promised at the altar. "But I didn't promise to tell a
lie," said Mrs. Trevelyan. And there were interviews between Lady
Milborough and Trevelyan, and interviews between Lady Milborough and
Nora Rowley. The poor dear old dowager was exceedingly busy and full
of groans, prescribing Naples, prescribing a course of extra prayers,
prescribing a general course of letting by-gones be by-gones,--to
which, however, Trevelyan would by no means assent without some
assurance, which he might regard as a guarantee,--prescribing
retirement to a small town in the west of France if Naples would not
suffice; but she could effect nothing.

Mrs. Trevelyan, indeed, did a thing which was sure of itself to
render any steps taken for a reconciliation ineffectual. In the midst
of all this turmoil,--while she and her husband were still living in
the same house, but apart because of their absurd quarrel respecting
Colonel Osborne, she wrote another letter to that gentleman. The
argument by which she justified this to herself, and to her sister
after it was done, was the real propriety of her own conduct
throughout her whole intimacy with Colonel Osborne. "But that is
just what Louis doesn't want you to do," Nora had said, filled with
anger and dismay. "Then let Louis give me an order to that effect,
and behave to me like a husband, and I will obey him," Emily had
answered. And she had gone on to plead that in her present condition
she was under no orders from her husband. She was left to judge for
herself, and,--judging for herself,--she knew, as she said, that it
was best that she should write to Colonel Osborne. Unfortunately
there was no ground for hoping that Colonel Osborne was ignorant
of this insane jealousy on the part of her husband. It was better,
therefore, she said, that she should write to him,--whom on the
occasion she took care to name to her sister as "papa's old
friend,"--and explain to him what she would wish him to do, and what
not to do. Colonel Osborne answered the letter very quickly, throwing
much more of demonstrative affection than he should have done into
his "Dear Emily," and his "Dearest Friend." Of course Mrs. Trevelyan
had burned this answer, and of course Mr. Trevelyan had been told of
the correspondence. His wife, indeed, had been especially careful
that there should be nothing secret about the matter,--that it should
be so known in the house that Mr. Trevelyan should be sure to hear
of it. And he had heard of it, and been driven almost mad by it. He
had flown off to Lady Milborough, and had reduced his old friend to
despair by declaring that, after all, he began to fear that his wife
was--was--was--infatuated by that d---- scoundrel. Lady Milborough
forgave the language, but protested that he was wrong in his
suspicion. "To continue to correspond with him after what I have said
to her!" exclaimed Trevelyan. "Take her to Naples at once,"--said
Lady Milborough;--"at once!" "And have him after me?" said Trevelyan.
Lady Milborough had no answer ready, and not having thought of
this looked very blank. "I should find it harder to deal with her
there even than here," continued Trevelyan. Then it was that Lady
Milborough spoke of the small town in the west of France, urging
as her reason that such a man as Colonel Osborne would certainly
not follow them there; but Trevelyan had become indignant at this,
declaring that if his wife's good name could be preserved in no other
manner than that, it would not be worth preserving at all. Then Lady
Milborough had begun to cry, and had continued crying for a very long
time. She was very unhappy,--as unhappy as her nature would allow
her to be. She would have made almost any sacrifice to bring the two
young people together;--would have willingly given her time, her
money, her labour in the cause;--would probably herself have gone
to the little town in the west of France, had her going been of any
service. But, nevertheless, after her own fashion, she extracted no
small enjoyment out of the circumstances of this miserable quarrel.

anchor_source.last_words: I am not fit to be his mother?
anchor_source.key_moment: Brief reunion with Emily and Louey
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"Wrong to restore a child to his mother? Oh, Louis, think of it. What must my life be without him,--or you?"

"Don't talk of me. It is too late for that."

"Not if you will be reasonable, Louis, and listen to me. Oh, heavens,
how ill you are!" As she said this she drew nearer to him, so that
her face was almost close to his. "Louis, come back; come back, and
let it all be forgotten. It shall be a dream, a horrid dream, and
nobody shall speak of it." He left his hand within hers and stood
looking into her face. He was well aware that his life since he had
left her had been one long hour of misery. There had been to him no
alleviation, no comfort, no consolation. He had not a friend left to
him. Even his satellite, the policeman, was becoming weary of him and
manifestly suspicious. The woman with whom he was now lodging, and
whose resources were infinitely benefited by his payments to her, had
already thrown out hints that she was afraid of him. And as he looked
at his wife, he knew that he loved her. Everything for him now was
hot and dry and poor and bitter. How sweet would it be again to sit
with her soft hand in his, to feel her cool brow against his own, to
have the comfort of her care, and to hear the music of loving words!
The companionship of his wife had once been to him everything in the
world; but now, for many months past, he had known no companion. She
bade him come to her, and look upon all this trouble as a dream not
to be mentioned. Could it be possible that it should be so, and that
they might yet be happy together,--perhaps in some distant country,
where the story of all their misery might not be known? He felt all
this truly and with a keen accuracy. If he were mad, he was not all
mad. "I will tell you of nothing that is past," said she, hanging to
him, and coming still nearer to him, and embracing his arm.

Could she have condescended to ask him not to tell her of the
past;--had it occurred to her so to word her request,--she might
perhaps have prevailed. But who can say how long the tenderness of
his heart would have saved him from further outbreak;--and whether
such prevailing on her part would have been of permanent service? As
it was, her words wounded him in that spot of his inner self which
was most sensitive,--on that spot from whence had come all his fury.
A black cloud came upon his brow, and he made an effort to withdraw
himself from her grasp. It was necessary to him that she should in
some fashion own that he had been right, and now she was promising
him that she would not tell him of his fault! He could not thus
swallow down all the convictions by which he had fortified himself to
bear the misfortunes which he had endured. Had he not quarrelled with
every friend he possessed on this score; and should he now stultify
himself in all those quarrels by admitting that he had been cruel,
unjust, and needlessly jealous? And did not truth demand of him that
he should cling to his old assurances? Had she not been disobedient,
ill-conditioned, and rebellious? Had she not received the man, both
him personally and his letters, after he had explained to her that
his honour demanded that it should not be so? How could he come into
such terms as those now proposed to him, simply because he longed
to enjoy the rich sweetness of her soft hand, to feel the fragrance
of her breath, and to quench the heat of his forehead in the cool
atmosphere of her beauty? "Why have you driven me to this by your
intercourse with that man?" he said. "Why, why, why did you do it?"

She was still clinging to him. "Louis," she said, "I am your wife."

"Yes; you are my wife."

"And will you still believe such evil of me without any cause?"

"There has been cause,--horrible cause. You must
repent,--repent,--repent."

"Heaven help me," said the woman, falling back from him, and
returning to the boy who was now seated in Lady Rowley's lap. "Mamma,
do you speak to him. What can I say? Would he think better of me were
I to own myself to have been guilty, when there has been no guilt, no
slightest fault? Does he wish me to purchase my child by saying that
I am not fit to be his mother?"

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At last the maniac was dead, and in his last moments he had made such
reparation as was in his power for the evil that he had done. With
that slight touch of his dry fevered lips he had made the assertion
on which was to depend the future peace and comfort of the woman whom
he had so cruelly misused. To her mind the acquittal was perfect;
but she never explained to human ears,--not even to those of her
sister,--the manner in which it had been given. Her life, as far as
we are concerned with it, has been told. For the rest, it cannot be
but that it should be better than that which was passed. If there be
any retribution for such sufferings in money, liberty, and outward
comfort, such retribution she possessed;--for all that had been his,
was now hers. He had once suggested what she should do, were she
ever to be married again; and she felt that of such a career there
could be no possibility. Anything but that! We all know that widows'
practices in this matter do not always tally with wives' vows; but,
as regards Mrs. Trevelyan, we are disposed to think that the promise
will be kept. She has her child, and he will give her sufficient
interest to make life worth having.

anchor_source.event_description: After objecting to Colonel Osborne's frequent visits, Louis speaks to Emily in an angry, accusing manner and immediately realizes he has insulted her, though he cannot bring himself to apologize at once.
anchor_source.first_words: It was, moreover, well known in
anchor_source.last_words: shown a disposition to comply with his wishes on this day.
anchor_source.key_moment: Calling Osborne a snake in the grass
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
It was, moreover, well known in London,--though not known at all
to Mrs. Trevelyan,--that this ancient Lothario had before this
made himself troublesome in more than one family. He was fond of
intimacies with married ladies, and perhaps was not averse to the
excitement of marital hostility. It must be remembered, however, that
the hostility to which allusion is here made was not the hostility
of the pistol or the horsewhip,--nor, indeed, was it generally the
hostility of a word of spoken anger. A young husband may dislike
the too-friendly bearing of a friend, and may yet abstain from that
outrage on his own dignity and on his wife, which is conveyed by a
word of suspicion. Louis Trevelyan having taken a strong dislike to
Colonel Osborne, and having failed to make his wife understand that
this dislike should have induced her to throw cold water upon the
Colonel's friendship, had allowed himself to speak a word which
probably he would have willingly recalled as soon as spoken. But
words spoken cannot be recalled, and many a man and many a woman who
has spoken a word at once regretted, are far too proud to express
that regret. So it was with Louis Trevelyan when he told his wife
that he did not wish Colonel Osborne to come so often to his house.
He had said it with a flashing eye and an angry tone; and though she
had seen the eye flash before, and was familiar with the angry tone,
she had never before felt herself to be insulted by her husband. As
soon as the word had been spoken Trevelyan had left the room, and had
gone down among his books. But when he was alone, he knew that he
had insulted his wife. He was quite aware that he should have spoken
to her gently, and have explained to her, with his arm round her
waist, that it would be better for both of them that this friend's
friendship should be limited. There is so much in a turn of the eye
and in the tone given to a word when such things have to be said,--so
much more of importance than in the words themselves. As Trevelyan
thought of this, and remembered what his manner had been, how much
anger he had expressed, how far he had been from having his arm round
his wife's waist as he spoke to her, he almost made up his mind to
go up-stairs and to apologise. But he was one to whose nature the
giving of any apology was repulsive. He could not bear to have to own
himself to have been wrong. And then his wife had been most provoking
in her manner to him. When he had endeavoured to make her understand
his wishes by certain disparaging hints which he had thrown out as to
Colonel Osborne, saying that he was a dangerous man, one who did not
show his true character, a snake in the grass, a man without settled
principles, and such like, his wife had taken up the cudgels for her
friend, and had openly declared that she did not believe a word of
the things that were alleged against him. "But still, for all that,
it is true," the husband had said. "I have no doubt that you think
so," the wife had replied. "Men do believe evil of one another, very
often. But you must excuse me if I say that I think you are mistaken.
I have known Colonel Osborne much longer than you have done, Louis,
and papa has always had the highest opinion of him." Then Mr.
Trevelyan had become very angry, and had spoken those words which
he could not recall. As he walked to and fro among his books
down-stairs, he almost felt that he ought to beg his wife's pardon.
He knew his wife well enough to be sure that she would not forgive
him unless he did so. He would do so, he thought, but not exactly
now. A moment would come in which it might be easier than at present.
He would be able to assure her when he went up to dress for dinner,
that he had meant no harm. They were going out to dine at the house
of a lady of rank, the Countess Dowager of Milborough, a lady
standing high in the world's esteem, of whom his wife stood a little
in awe; and he calculated that this feeling, if it did not make his
task easy would yet take from it some of its difficulty. Emily would
be, not exactly cowed, by the prospect of Lady Milborough's dinner,
but perhaps a little reduced from her usual self-assertion. He would
say a word to her when he was dressing, assuring her that he had not
intended to animadvert in the slightest degree upon her own conduct.


   [Illustration: Shewing how wrath began.]


Luncheon was served, and the two ladies went down into the
dining-room. Mr. Trevelyan did not appear. There was nothing in
itself singular in that, as he was accustomed to declare that
luncheon was a meal too much in the day, and that a man should eat
nothing beyond a biscuit between breakfast and dinner. But he would
sometimes come in and eat his biscuit standing on the hearth-rug,
and drink what he would call half a quarter of a glass of sherry. It
would probably have been well that he should have done so now; but
he remained in his library behind the dining-room, and when his wife
and his sister-in-law had gone up-stairs, he became anxious to learn
whether Colonel Osborne would come on that day, and, if so, whether
he would be admitted. He had been told that Nora Rowley was to be
called for by another lady, a Mrs. Fairfax, to go out and look at
pictures. His wife had declined to join Mrs. Fairfax's party, having
declared that, as she was going to dine out, she would not leave
her baby all the afternoon. Louis Trevelyan, though he strove to
apply his mind to an article which he was writing for a scientific
quarterly review, could not keep himself from anxiety as to this
expected visit from Colonel Osborne. He was not in the least jealous.
He swore to himself fifty times over that any such feeling on his
part would be a monstrous injury to his wife. Nevertheless he knew
that he would be gratified if on that special day Colonel Osborne
should be informed that his wife was not at home. Whether the man
were admitted or not, he would beg his wife's pardon; but he could,
he thought, do so with more thorough efficacy and affection if she
should have shown a disposition to comply with his wishes on this
day.

anchor_source.event_description: Louis orders the servant Richard to tell Colonel Osborne that Mrs. Trevelyan is 'not at home' if he calls again. He gives the instruction in an indifferent tone, but feels thoroughly ashamed of it as he says it.
anchor_source.first_words: So he kissed her again, and had
anchor_source.last_words: the remainder of the dinner passed off almost in silence.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
So he kissed her again, and had the boy brought into the room, and by
the time that he went to dress for dinner he was able, at any rate,
to seem to be well pleased.

"Richard," he said to the servant, as soon as he was down-stairs,
"when Colonel Osborne calls again, say that your mistress is--not at
home." He gave the order in the most indifferent tone of voice which
he could assume; but as he gave it he felt thoroughly ashamed of it.
Richard, who, with the other servants, had of course known that there
had been a quarrel between his master and mistress for the last two
days, no doubt understood all about it.

While they were sitting at dinner on the next day, a Saturday, there
came another note from Colonel Osborne. The servant brought it to
his mistress, and she, when she had looked at it, put it down by her
plate. Trevelyan knew immediately from whom the letter had come, and
understood how impossible it was for his wife to give it up in the
servant's presence. The letter lay there till the man was out of the
room, and then she handed it to Nora. "Will you give that to Louis?"
she said. "It comes from the man whom he supposes to be my lover."

"Emily!" said he, jumping from his seat, "how can you allow words so
horrible and so untrue to fall from your mouth?"

"If it be not so, why am I to be placed in such a position as this?
The servant knows, of course, from whom the letter comes, and sees
that I have been forbidden to open it." Then the man returned to the
room, and the remainder of the dinner passed off almost in silence.

probes.scenario: At a small evening gathering, Colonel Osborne crosses the room and, before others can hear, says he wishes to send Emily a brief note on a family matter and asks Louis to let it pass through his hands if that seems proper. Osborne waits for his answer.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan answer Osborne in that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws himself up and refuses the request with cold civility.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, Colonel Osborne; I cannot undertake any such office between you and my wife.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He sees Osborne's approach as unwarranted freedom, but still as something a firm husband may check by ordinary rule. The point is propriety; he tells himself it is not jealousy, only plain decency.

voice.note: This fits early Louis well: the coldly formal refusal, emphasis on propriety and a husband's ordinary authority, and the self-exculpating insistence that it is not jealousy all suit his initial suspicion without importing later obsession.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames Osborne as a morally improper social concern to be checked by ordinary propriety—explicitly 'not jealousy'—rather than as an enemy whose contact must be pursued as proof of injury.

phase_responses.gt_action: He blocks the exchange and keeps his eyes on Osborne, as though weighing what more may lie behind it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: There shall be no note, and no message. I desire that your intercourse with Mrs. Trevelyan should cease.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The request itself looks like proof that Osborne will press in by any opening left him. Louis reads even this guarded proposal as contamination trying to enter his house under a decent phrase.

voice.note: This fits Louis in chapter-15 territory: the speech is stiff, proprietary, and controlling, and the thought plausibly shows him treating even a seemingly proper request as an intrusive, contaminating opening without relying on later knowledge or anachronistic language.

phase_fit.note: Louis treats even a guarded note request as contaminating access that must be blocked, focusing on policing Osborne's contact with Emily rather than on a fully settled symbolic-enemy grievance.

phase_responses.gt_action: He turns from courtesy and treats the request as an insult, refusing with open hostility.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You have no right to name my wife to me, sir. Send nothing; attempt nothing.
phase_responses.gt_thought: To Louis, Osborne's guilt is already settled, and this quiet application is only another shape of the same dishonor. He does not examine the matter; he receives it as fresh outrage from the man who has ruined his peace.

voice.note: The refusal and inward certainty fit Louis at chapter 49, with Osborne treated not as a mere impropriety but as an already-convicted enemy, and the diction remains plausible to Trollope's world.

phase_fit.note: The thought makes Osborne's guilt feel already settled and interprets even a modest request as another form of established dishonor, which matches the fixed-enemy logic of Phase 2 more than mere policing of contact.

phase_responses.gt_action: He fixes Osborne with a worn, bitter stare and gives a broken refusal.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No. You have done enough. Let her alone.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old grievance rises with hardly any need of cause; Osborne remains the corrupter in his mind, even now. Louis has little strength for dispute, but the enemy's place is fixed, and every approach seems part of the injury that never ended.

voice.note: The worn bitterness, curt refusal, and fixed sense of Osborne as a lasting corrupter fit Louis's post-collapse hostility by chapter 83, and the language stays broadly period-appropriate and in character.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly presents Osborne as a fixed enemy carried forward with little fresh cause and with Louis too weakened for active pursuit, which matches persistent post-collapse hostility.

probes.scenario: At a factory benefit supper, Louis Trevelyan sees Colonel Osborne step aside with Emily and hand her a folded note after a low, familiar word. Several people notice; when Emily turns back, the note is still in her glove.
probes.question: How does Louis Trevelyan respond to seeing that exchange?

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis goes to Emily afterward and asks, in private, to see the note and hear why Osborne thought fit to send it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I do not like that man's ways. Let me see what he has written.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Osborne's manner is slippery, and a husband has a right to object to underhand familiarity. Louis still tells himself this is plain propriety, not jealousy.

voice.note: This fits Louis's early suspicious, self-justifying hostility well: the private demand, dislike of Osborne's 'ways,' and insistence on propriety rather than jealousy are all phase-appropriate, with no clear knowledge leak or anachronistic diction for the period.

phase_fit.note: He frames Osborne as morally improper and asks for an ordinary private explanation, while explicitly construing his reaction as propriety rather than jealousy or a settled enemy campaign.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis takes the note from Emily, reads it, and tells her Osborne is not to address her again except through him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: This ends here. He has no business writing to you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The note is not a trifle but another taint from Osborne's presence, one more liberty taken because he has been allowed too near. Louis reads contact itself as evidence that something foul is pushing in.

voice.note: This fits Louis in phase 1: he treats Osborne's mere contact as contaminating proof, speaks in controlling proprietary terms, and nothing in the wording or thought depends on knowledge beyond chapter 15 or jars badly with the early-20th-century setting.

phase_fit.note: He treats Osborne's note and mere proximity as contaminating evidence that must be policed and cut off, which matches the phase where Louis actively controls access, letters, and contact rather than merely voicing principled suspicion or sustaining a fully fixed grievance.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis pockets the note and leaves the supper to find out who saw Osborne arrive, meaning to trace every part of the meeting.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Keep his paper if you like; I know what sort of man sends it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: For Louis, Osborne's guilt no longer waits on the contents of any message; the note merely confirms an injury already settled in his mind. He fastens on Osborne as the author of his humiliation and hunts for facts to pin it down.

voice.note: This fits Louis in phase 2: the speech is bitterly condemnatory, the action shows his settled need to investigate and fix Osborne as the cause of injury, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate with no clear knowledge beyond chapter 49.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly says Osborne's guilt is already settled and that Louis uses the note only to confirm and pin down a preexisting grievance, which is the hallmark of the fixed symbolic enemy phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: Louis stares at the note in Emily's glove and mutters Osborne's name, refusing the supper talk around him.

phase_responses.gt_thought: The old grievance rises whole, needing no fresh proof and no workable plan. Even in weakness, Louis feels Osborne as the lingering corrupter, the fixed figure left behind by all the ruin.
